passage: Rain had flooded the playground, so the whole class was squeezed into the school hall for games period. Kashish, nine, had her hopscotch rules ready: left foot first, no touching lines, three turns each. When the others suggested a new game called islands, her face crumpled. "No! We always play hopscotch on Thursdays!" Baljeet ma'am knelt beside her. "The rain changed our plan. Here's the new plan: ten minutes of islands, then ten minutes of your hopscotch. I'll keep time on my watch." Kashish watched the watch for all ten minutes of islands, arms folded. Then she played hopscotch, and at the end she said, "Islands again next week? With my rules for the jumping."

qa.q: What was Kashish's first hopscotch rule?
qa.a: Left foot first.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's face crumple when the others suggested islands?
qa.a: The change felt scary to her, since she expects hopscotch on Thursdays and fixed rules make her feel safe.

qa.q: What did Baljeet ma'am do that helped Kashish cope, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gave a clear new plan with set times on her watch, so the change felt predictable and Kashish could manage it.

qa.q: How might the other children feel if Kashish always insisted on her rules?
qa.a: They might feel frustrated or left out, which is why a shared, timed plan helps everyone.

grounding: On a rainy day, a nine-year-old clings to fixed game rules, and a teacher's calm, predictable plan helps her loosen them.

passage: In the narrow lane outside their Mumbai chawl, Dhruv, ten, had a rule for everything in gully cricket: one-tip-one-hand, no running on the gutter side, and he always batted first. When Ujjwal said, "Let's do double runs today," Dhruv threw the bat down. "Then I'm not playing!" He stomped upstairs. His mother didn't scold. That evening she helped the boys make a chart: each day one old rule stays fixed, and one new rule gets tried. Dhruv read it three times. The next day he stood at the crease, jaw tight, while Ujjwal announced, "New rule: double runs." Dhruv took a breath. "Okay. But one-tip-one-hand stays." "Deal."

qa.q: What new rule did Ujjwal suggest?
qa.a: Ujjwal suggested double runs.

qa.q: What might Dhruv be feeling when he throws the bat down?
qa.a: He likely feels upset and unsafe when the familiar rules change, so he wants to stop playing.

qa.q: What choice did his mother make, and why does it suit Dhruv?
qa.a: She made a chart where one rule stays fixed and one new rule is tried each day, giving him predictable structure so change feels manageable.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel when Dhruv says "Okay" the next day?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably feels relieved and pleased that the game can go on with something new.

grounding: A ten-year-old insists on his own cricket rules and storms off at a change, and his mother's predictable chart helps him accept one new rule.

passage: Playground note, Class 3, Thursday. Omkar, new since his family moved in March, tried to run the whole tag game again. "You have to touch the tree, not the wall! And only I say when it starts!" When Shalini changed the base to the swings, he shouted, kicked the sand and walked off. I have noticed he does this most on days his mother is late for pickup. So I have started a fixed game-time routine for the class: same place, rules on a chart, one new rule allowed only on Fridays. Today he let Shalini's swing base stay, arms crossed but playing. Next step: I will invite him to help write Friday's new rule.

qa.q: Where did Shalini move the base?
qa.a: To the swings.

qa.q: What might Omkar be feeling when the base changes?
qa.a: He seems anxious and angry, since fixed rules help him feel safe after a big move.

qa.q: Which of the note-writer's steps is helping, and why?
qa.a: The fixed routine with rules on a chart, because predictable structure lets Omkar loosen his grip.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Omkar kicks the sand and walks off?
qa.a: Shalini may feel confused or annoyed, since she only suggested a new base.

grounding: Shows a child who insists on fixed rules in games, with an adult using calm, predictable structure to help him loosen control.

passage:
Sunday. Dilnaz came over and wanted to play Ludo her way, where you don't need a six to start. That's NOT the rule. I told her, and she said it's more fun, and I said then go and play at your house. She went home. Now I feel bad. I don't know why I get so upset when rules change. It's like when Papa's job changed and we had to move and nothing was the same. At least in Ludo I know what happens. Mumma said tomorrow we can make a rule chart with Dilnaz: my rule on Monday, her rule on Tuesday. Maybe I can try hers once. Once.
Vasudha

qa.q: What was Dilnaz's rule for Ludo?
qa.a: You don't need a six to start.

qa.q: How does Vasudha feel after Dilnaz goes home?
qa.a: Vasudha feels bad and guilty, and confused about getting so upset over a changed rule.

qa.q: Why might Mumma's rule chart help?
qa.a: It gives a clear, predictable plan, so trying Dilnaz's rule feels safer.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when told to go home?
qa.a: Dilnaz was probably hurt and surprised, since she only wanted to make the game more fun.

grounding: Illustrates a child who clings to fixed game rules for safety after a big change, with a predictable plan helping.

passage: Behind the panchayat office in a village near Jhansi, Nikita drew the hopscotch squares with a stick and explained the rules, all nine of them, to Afreen and the Yadav twins. Stones must land exactly inside. No hopping on the lines. Nikita goes first. When Afreen suggested a double jump at the end, Nikita's face went red. "No! That's wrong!" She stamped on the squares, smudging them. Since her Baba had gone to work in the city, Nikita had been like this about everything: the same route to school, the same seat, the same rules. Her Dadi, watching from the charpai, called her over. "Same time every evening, you girls play here. Nikita's rules today. Afreen's one new rule tomorrow." Nikita chewed her lip, then nodded.

qa.q: How many rules did Nikita explain?
qa.a: All nine of them.

qa.q: What might Nikita be feeling when Afreen suggests a double jump?
qa.a: She seems anxious and angry, since fixed rules feel safe while her Baba is away.

qa.q: Why is Dadi's plan a good one?
qa.a: It gives a calm, predictable structure, with one new rule on a set day, so change feels manageable.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel when Nikita smudges the squares?
qa.a: Afreen likely feels startled and hurt that a small idea caused such anger.

grounding: Shows a child insisting on fixed game rules for safety during uncertainty, and an elder offering calm, predictable structure.

passage:
In the courtyard of their Istanbul apartment block, Selin had drawn the hopscotch squares herself, perfectly straight. "You have to hop on your left foot on seven. That's the rule."
Hana skipped seven. "Let's make it more fun. We can jump anywhere!"
Selin's face crumpled. "No! Then it's not the game!" She stamped off and sat on the steps, arms tight around her knees.
Her mother had noticed that since the moving boxes appeared in the hall, Selin had been making more rules for everything.
Later, her mother suggested something. "Every game starts the same way: you both say the rules out loud first. And at the end, you can each choose one new rule for next time."
The next day, Selin said the rules. Then, a little nervously, she let Hana add one: "Clap on number ten."

qa.q: Which foot did Selin's rule say to hop on at seven?
qa.a: The left foot.

qa.q: How did Selin feel when Hana changed the rules?
qa.a: She felt upset and unsettled; her face crumpled, she stamped off and hugged her knees on the steps.

qa.q: Why might her mother's idea help Selin loosen her rules?
qa.a: Saying the rules at the start and adding one new rule at the end gives a calm, predictable structure, so change feels safer.

qa.q: How might Hana see Selin's strict rules?
qa.a: Hana just wanted to make the game more fun, so she may feel confused or bossed about when Selin gets so upset.

grounding: Shows a child who insists on fixed game rules when her world feels uncertain, and how a calm, predictable structure helps loosen them.
